cards.front: What three components make up a nucleotide?
cards.back: A **nucleotide** contains a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogen-containing base.

cards.front: Why does the base sequence on one DNA strand determine the sequence on the other strand?
cards.back: Each base can only pair with one partner: adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine (**complementary base pairing**), so one strand fixes the other.
cards.hint: Consider which base each one can bond to.

cards.front: What does semi-conservative mean for DNA replication?
cards.back: Each new DNA molecule contains **one original strand and one newly made strand**.
cards.hint: Think about how many old strands each daughter molecule keeps.

cards.front: Which pentose sugar do DNA nucleotides contain?
cards.back: **Deoxyribose**, which has one fewer oxygen atom than the ribose found in RNA nucleotides.

cards.front: Which base do RNA nucleotides use in place of thymine?
cards.back: **Uracil**. RNA nucleotides contain ribose and uracil, while DNA nucleotides use thymine.

cards.front: What is the base sequence of the new strand made from the template strand TAGC?
cards.back: **ATCG**. Each template base pairs with its partner: T with A, A with T, G with C and C with G.
cards.hint: Pair each template base with its complementary base.

cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds hold an adenine–thymine pair together?
cards.back: **Two**. Cytosine–guanine pairs form three. Each bond is weak, but many together stabilise the molecule.

cards.front: What does it mean that the two DNA strands are antiparallel?
cards.back: The **antiparallel** strands run in opposite directions, with each sugar–phosphate backbone on the outside and the bases facing inwards.
cards.hint: Think about the direction each strand runs.

cards.front: What are the main steps of DNA replication, in order?
cards.back: 1 Hydrogen bonds between bases break and the strands separate. 2 Each original strand acts as a template. 3 Free nucleotides pair with exposed bases. 4 New nucleotides are joined into strands, giving two DNA molecules with the original sequence.
cards.hint: Start with what must happen before any copying can begin.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say semi-conservative means one DNA molecule is entirely old and the other entirely new?
cards.back: Each daughter molecule contains both an old strand and a new strand. Neither molecule is wholly old or wholly new.

cards.front: What does DNA helicase do during replication?
cards.back: It **separates** the two strands by breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing bases on both template strands.
cards.hint: Consider the first step of replication.

cards.front: Where can DNA polymerase add nucleotides to a growing strand?
cards.back: Only to the **growing end** of a strand, so new DNA is always made in one direction.
cards.hint: Think about where new nucleotides can attach.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say DNA polymerase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases?
cards.back: Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases. Polymerase forms bonds in the new sugar–phosphate backbone, joining nucleotides together.
cards.hint: Compare the job of each enzyme.

cards.front: How does the antiparallel arrangement affect the making of the two new strands?
cards.back: One new strand grows continuously towards the opening point. The other is made in short sections, which **DNA ligase** joins together.
